titleStmt.title: Fixed-Priority Schedulability of Arbitrary-Deadline Sporadic Tasks upon Periodic Resources

analytic.title: Fixed-Priority Schedulability of Arbitrary-Deadline Sporadic Tasks upon Periodic Resources

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Schedulability for compositional real-time systems has been the focus of a great deal of recent research. In this problem domain, we consider the fixed-priority (FP) scheduling of arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems upon periodic resources. Existing exact or approximate schedulability tests for dedicated uniprocessor scheduling can be used in this setting by modeling the "no-supply period" of the periodic resource model as a special highest priority task. However, the exact schedulability test is highly inefficient from computational perspective, and the straightforward approximate test is pessimistic due to the approximation on the resource unavailability along with the resource demand. In this paper, along with obtaining an exact characterization of schedulability for this setting, we address the need for efficient and effective schedulability results for the large and important class of arbitrary-deadline task systems by deriving a polynomialtime sufficient schedulability algorithm. By simulations, we show that this algorithm performs very well compared with the exact test, and even better than the approximate test.

div.head: I. Introduction
div.p: Over the last decade, compositional real-time research has become one of the emerging trends in embedded realtime systems due to the increasing scale and complexity of such systems. In this design paradigm, a large system is decomposed into smaller and simpler components, and developed independently. The major benefit of these systems is achieved by component abstraction, which hides the internal complexity and details of one component from developers of other components. In most real-time compositional frameworks, a component uses a real-time interface to quantify its resource requirements. Therefore, given a compositional framework and a real-time interface, a fundamental research challenge for such systems is to derive efficient schedulability analysis techniques for realtime guarantee verification of the components and the system as a whole.

For this paper, we consider the general explicit-deadline periodic resource (EDP) model [7] as our compositional framework. An EDP resource Ω is characterized by a three-tuple (Π, Θ, Δ) where a component C executed upon Ω is guaranteed Θ (capacity) units of processing resource supply for successive Π-length intervals (period of repetition) within Δ (relative deadline) time units after the start of the Π-length interval. The "no-supply period" of Ω is the duration of time at which the component C does not receive any processing resource; i.e., Π -Θ units of time in any Π-interval of time in this case.

We are interested in the setting where a component is modeled as a set of sporadic tasks [15] and scheduled by preemptive fixed-priority (FP) scheduling algorithm upon the EDP resource. A sporadic task τ i = (e i , d i , p i ) is characterized by a worst-case execution requirement e i , a (relative) deadline d i , and a minimum inter-arrival separation p i . Prior works on this setting have considered either implicit-deadline tasks (i.e., relative deadlines equal periods) or constrained-deadline tasks (i.e., relative deadlines are at most periods). However, the infrequently addressed arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems (i.e., no restriction on the relationship between the period and relative deadline) are a standard and oft-used task model for traditional real-time systems.

In the above setting, existing schedulability results for dedicated uniprocessor system [9], [12], [16] can be applied. A component consisting of sporadic tasks and scheduled upon periodic resource can be converted to an equivalent task system scheduled upon a dedicated resource by modeling the "no-supply period" of the periodic resource model as a special highest priority task [17]. However, the exact solution obtained in this approach is highly inefficient computationally, which makes this test impractical for real-time open system environment where applications may join or leave the system dynamically. Furthermore, the approximate solution is pessimistic due to the straightforward approximation of the resource unavailability period along with the approximation of the resource demand, and thus, over-estimates resource capacity. Therefore, the lack of efficient schedulability tests for arbitrarydeadline tasks in this setting represents a fundamental gap in our understanding of periodic resource schedulability. In this paper we aim to extend schedulability theory for this larger class of tasks and derive a sufficient algorithm for this setting. §Our Contribution. We characterize a new exact schedulability condition (Theorem 1) for arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems scheduled by a fixed-priority (e.g., ratemonotonic or deadline-monotonic) algorithm upon an EDP resource model. To address the computational inefficiency of the exact test, we derive a parametric polynomialtime sufficient schedulability algorithm. Furthermore, we evaluate the effectiveness of our algorithm by simulation over randomly-generated task systems, and show that our approach performs very well compared with the exact test, and better than the approximate test. §Organization. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we briefly review the current literature on fixed-priority scheduling and compositional real-time frameworks. In Section III, we provide necessary notations required for the rest of the paper and give the exact schedulability condition. In Section IV, we present a sufficient schedulability algorithm and prove its correctness. We give simulation results in Section V.

div.head: II. Related Work
div.p: The concept of compositional systems was first introduced by Deng and Liu [5] in their work real-time open environments and Rajkumar et al. [18] in their work resource kernels. Feng and Mok [8] proposed the concept of temporal partitions to support hierarchical sharing of a processing resource. Shin et al. [19] proposed the related periodic resource model to characterize the supply guaranteed to any component in compositional system, which was generalized by Easwaran et al. [7] to explicit deadline periodic (EDP) resource model. For the temporal partition models where components are scheduled by fixed-priority, Lipari and Bini [13] proposed exact, pseudo-polynomial time algorithm for resource allocation, and Almeida and Pedreiras [1] proposed sufficient, polynomial-time resource allocation techniques.

The resource allocation for fixed-priority scheduled periodic resource model has been previously studied for constrained deadline case. An exact solution based on exact schedulability techniques for uniprocessor real-time systems has been proposed by Easwaran et al. [7] for EDP resource. Shin and Lee [20] proposed an O(n)time sufficient solution for periodic resource (Π equals Δ). In our prior work [6], we gave an approximate resource allocation algorithm for EDP resource. The schedulability analysis of fixed-priority-scheduled components upon periodic resources can be compared to existing fixed-priority servers [11], [21], [22] used to serve the aperiodic jobs in the system. By modeling the "no-supply period" of the periodic resource model as a special task (similar to the aperiodic server job), traditional uniprocessor schedulability analysis can be applied. Using this approach, in [17], Okwudire et al. gave a linear-time sufficient schedulability test for fixed-priority scheduled component with harmonic task periods for two-level hierarchical system.

For fixed-priority scheduled systems on dedicated uniprocessor platforms where tasks have arbitrarydeadlines, Lehoczky [12] provided an exact feasibility test, and Fisher and Baruah [9] proposed a polynomial time approximate test. However, the existence of any work for any of the real-time compositional frameworks with FP-schedulability analysis where components are sporadic tasks with arbitrary-deadline and period is unknown. The goal of our work is to fill this needed gap by obtaining an efficient algorithm for this large and important class of tasks scheduled upon periodic resource model with preemptive uniprocessor platforms.

div.head: III. Model and Notation
div.p: In this section, we present background and notation for the task model, workload functions, and periodic resource model that we use throughout the paper. Furthermore, we state exact conditions for an arbitrary-deadline sporadic task system to be schedulable upon an EDP resource.

§Sporadic Task Model. Recall the definition of a sporadic task given in the introduction. A sporadic task system τ = {τ 1 , . . . , τ n } is a collection of n such sporadic tasks. For any task τ i ∈ τ , we denote j-th job of τ i by τ i,j . We will assume an arbitrary-deadline sporadic task systems; that is, no restriction is placed on the relationship between d i and p i (i.e., a task τ i ∈ τ might have d i ≥ p i ). The task utilization for a sporadic task τ i is defined as u i = e i /p i . The system utilization is denoted by U (τ ) = τi∈τ u i . We will assume that U (τ ) ≤ 1; otherwise, task system τ cannot be scheduled (by any algorithm) to meet all deadlines upon a dedicated preemptive uniprocessor. We denote max{0, x} by (x) 0 .

Each task in the task system has a fixed-priority and tasks are indexed in non-increasing priority order. That is, τ i has higher (or equal) priority than τ j , if and only if, i ≤ j. As tasks generate jobs, each job inherits the priority of its generating task (i.e., all jobs generated by task τ i have the same priority as τ i ). When multiple jobs of same task are ready to execute, the job with lowest index (arrival time) gets to execute first. For this paper, we assume each component uses FP-scheduling as the componentlevel scheduling algorithm. Whenever component C is allocated the processor, C executes the highest-priority job with remaining execution; ties are broken in favor of the job generated from the lower task index. There is currently no known optimal fixed-priority scheduling algorithm for arbitrary relative deadlines. In [2], Audsley proposed an optimal priority assignment algorithm.

§Workload Functions. To determine the schedulability of a sporadic task system, it is often useful to quantify the maximum amount of execution time requested by the task in its worst-case phasing over any given interval. For sporadic task systems, it is known that the worstcase phasing is the synchronous arrival sequence. The synchronous arrival sequence occurs when all tasks of a sporadic task system release jobs at the same time instant and subsequent jobs as soon as permissible. We denote the synchronous arrival of τ i,j by a ij = (j-1)•p i and absolute deadline of a job τ i,j by d ij = (j -1) • p i + d i . Lehoczky et al. [10] defined request-bound function to characterize the execution requests of any task τ i .

Definition 1 (Request-Bound Function): For any t > 0 and sporadic task τ i , the request-bound function (RBF) quantifies the maximum cumulative execution requests that could be generated by jobs of τ i arriving within a contiguous time-interval of length t. For sporadic tasks, RBF can be calculated as follows [10].
div.formula: RBF(τ i , t) def = t p i • e i .(1)
div.p: The request-bound function for a sporadic task τ i is a right continuous function with discontinuities at time points of the form t ≡ a • p i where a ∈ N. The cumulative requestbound function for τ i,j is defined as follows:
div.formula: W i,j (t) def = je i + i-1 h=1 RBF(τ h , t).(2)
div.p: This function quantifies the total execution requests of all tasks of higher priority than τ i over the interval (0, t] and the execution request of the first j jobs of τ i . In sporadic or synchronous periodic task system with relative deadline bounded by periods, it is necessary and sufficient to only check the response time of the first job of each task. That is, τ is schedulable on a uniprocessor iff τ i,1 has a worst case response time at most d i for all τ i ∈ τ [3], [14].

When deadlines can exceed periods, it is no longer sufficient to check the response-times of only the first job of each task [12]. Instead, it is potentially necessary to check the response-time of all the jobs in synchronous level-i busy interval for each task τ i . Lehoczky [12] showed that the synchronous level-i (defined below) is the longest possible busy interval.

Definition 2 (Dedicated Synchronous Level-i Busy Interval): A level-i busy interval upon a dedicated preemptive uniprocessor platform is a time interval [0, B i ) where only jobs of {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ i } are executing continuously and the following is true:
1) All tasks of {τ1, τ2, . . . , τi} release jobs at time zero.

2) Each task of {τ1, τ2, . . . , τi} releases tasks periodically (i.e., τ k ∈ {τ1, τ2, . . . , τi} has successive job releases p k time units apart). 3) Bi is the first time instant such that all jobs of Ti released in the interval [0, Bi) have completed.
The exact schedulability condition for arbitrarydeadline fixed-priority scheduling in preemptive uniprocessor platform is given by the following equation.

div.p: §Exact EDP Resource Schedulability. While an exact schedulability test for EDP resource can be derived from dedicated uniprocessor schedulability test, we characterize a new exact test, which will be useful for derivation of the efficient test presented in this paper. In the EDP resource model, the processor is no longer dedicated to a single subsystem, but shared among components. The length of a level-i busy interval for a task system τ now depends upon the amount of processing time that a resource Ω can provide to τ over that interval. Thus, we cannot use Equation 7 to directly evaluate FP-schedulability upon Ω. Instead, we need to redefine the level-i busy interval to account for the effects of Ω's resource parameters.

Definition 7 (Synchronous Level-i Busy Interval for Ω): A level-i busy interval upon an EDP resource Ω = (Π, Θ, Δ) is a time interval [0, B Ω i ) where only jobs of {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ i } are execute upon Ω and the following conditions hold:

div.head: Scheduled Arbitrary-Deadline Tasks
div.p: In this section, we give our schedulability algorithm for arbitrary-deadline sporadic tasks on an EDP resource called AFPSCHEDULABILITY (Section IV-A) with a formal proof correctness (Section IV-B).

div.head: A. Description
div.p: The pseudocode of our sufficient algorithm AFPSCHEDULABILITY is presented in Algorithm 1, along with an auxiliary functions AFPSINTERSTAGE, given in Algorithms 2. AFPSCHEDULABILITY works as follows. For each task τ i ∈ τ , we try to determine which jobs τ i,j in the synchronous level-i busy interval for Ω can complete by their deadline, starting with j = 1. We check job schedulability by considering each of the testing set points t a ∈ S i (τ, k) (in increasing order) and then incrementing j once we have determined that the previous job (or jobs) are schedulable. For each testing point t a and current job τ i,j for which we are trying to determine schedulability, we consider the corresponding line segment L i,j ta . Line 5 informally checks whether an intersection between L i,j ta and sbf is in the interval (t a-1 , t a ]. If not, we check (Line 6) whether τ i,j 's deadline elapses in the interval (t a-1 , t a ], in which case we declare that the system is not schedulable.

In the case that L i,j ta intersects with sbf over (t a-1 , t a ], we determine the intersection point of L i,j ta with the i,j tastep of the sbf in Line 10. Line 12 checks whether this intersection occurs prior to τ i,j 's deadline. If so, we then calculate in Line 15 the number of jobs after τ i,j that complete execution (not necessarily by their deadline) in the interval (t a-1 , t a ]. Line 16 determines (via AFPSINTERSTAGE) whether these jobs will meet their deadline and returns not schedulable, if they do not. Each iteration of the "inner" loop of AFPSCHEDULABILITY from Lines 4 to 25 requires constant time (including the auxiliary function). At the beginning of the inner loop, all the jobs from 1 to j -1 are schedulable. Initialization When j = 1, there is no job in the range 1 to j -1. We can conclude that all job in that range is schedulable (trivially).

Maintenance At each loop iteration, we are starting with τ i,j , which is the lowest active job in the interval (t a-1 , t a ] (has arrival at or before t a-1 and deadline after t a-1 ). All the jobs from 1 to j -1 are schedulable. If any of them missed deadline, the algorithm would not have continued to j-th job. Now we need to show after current iteration we have successfully checked schedulability of the jobs that are active within current interval (t a-1 , t a ]. We check the schedulability condition for the first active job (τ i,j ) in the interval (Line 5 to 13). At the end of the loop we check if all the jobs of τ i available in the system have meet their execution requirement, and terminate the loop (Line 18) for this case.

Termination The loop terminates when all intervals of testing set points have been considered, or the busy interval for task τ i have ended. As the loop did not return Not Schedulable, all the jobs from 1 to j -1 are schedulable.
The outer loop checks the schedulability condition for each task in the task system.

div.head: V. Simulation
div.p: We compared our proposed algorithm with the exact and the approximate schedulability tests for arbitrarydeadline FP-scheduled task system with EDP resource. From the compositional system scheduled upon EDP resource, we obtained an equivalent dedicated uniprocessor system for each component by adding a special highest priority task to the task system τ , which represents the "no-supply period" of the EDP resource (similar to [17]). Then we performed the exact [12] and the approximate [9] schedulability test for dedicated uniprocessor system to the modified task system. We have considered a fixed resource period Π and deadline Δ, and computed minimum capacity Θ required to schedule the system for the three tests. The simulation parameters and value ranges are shown below: 1) Task system size n = 10; k is set in the range [1,20]; Π is set to 10 and Δ is equal to Π. 2) U (τ ) is taken from the range [0.1, 0.9] at 0.05-increments and individual task utilizations ui are generated using UUniFast algorithm [4]. 3) Each τi ∈ τ , period pi is uniformly drawn from the interval [5,30], deadline di is uniformly drawn from [5,100] and execution time ei is set to ui.pi. 4) The component-level scheduler is rate-monotonic. 5) A 2.2GHz Intel Core i7-2670QM CPU with 8Gb RAM is used. Each point in the plot represents 1000 simulation runs.

For each simulation, given task system size n and system utilization U (τ ), we randomly generated taskset parameters u i , p i , d i , for each task τ i . Then we executed a binary search to search for minimum capacity in the range [0, Π], using each of the schedulability test as subroutines to generate exact, approximate and sufficient (i.e., AFPSFEASIBILITY) solutions. In Fig. 5 the capacity obtained from the three algorithms are plotted against system utilization. We observe that the sufficient test performs better than the approximate test. In Fig. 6, the execution time (in log scale) for the three algorithms are plotted against task system utilization. Note that the capacity Θ is chosen considering the resource starvation period (i.e., Θ ≥ Π/2) and since task deadlines can exceed task periods, the iterative exact algorithm converges quickly for lower system utilization. However, for higher system utilization, the execution time of the sufficient test outperforms the other two tests. The last plot shown in Fig. 7 compares the relative error of the approximate and the sufficient algorithm with respect to the exact algorithm. We observe that the relative error for the approximate algorithm (0.48 to 0.23) is almost twice as that of the sufficient algorithm (0.28 to 0.12).

div.head: VI. Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we devised a sufficient schedulability test for compositional real-time systems with fixedpriority component-level scheduling algorithms. For a set of arbitrary-deadline tasks as a component scheduled upon explicit-deadline periodic resource, our algorithm runs in polynomial time. We verified our result by running simulation over synthetically generated tasks, and showed that our algorithm is competitive with exact test with an increasing efficiency especially for higher system utilizations, and performs better in efficiency and relative error compared to the straightforward approximate test. Future work will attempt to extend the results for the arbitrarydeadline tasks to other compositional frameworks as well as multiprocessor platforms.
